transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
China's top leader Xi Jinping will meet President Trump tomorrow in Washington.
NPR's Emily Feng reports their meeting comes at a crucial time for both men.
For China, the priority here is to keep the U.S. pacified without committing to anything.
For the U.S., there's been an overall lack of direction in the Trump administration's
approach to China this term, says Eli Ratner, a former assistant secretary of defense in
the Biden administration.
They have moved away from that declaratory policy around seeing China as the dominant
strategic competitor.
They have unwound some of the traditional support that we've had toward Taiwan and
other allies and partners.
A senior administration official said Trump will personally meet Xi on the tarmac at Joint
Base Andrews as he arrives in the U.S., a sign of the importance of the visit to the
president.
Emily Feng, NPR News, Washington.
A federal judge holds a hearing today on three media organizations' lawsuit against the
federal government.
CNN, MS Now, and Politico want to overturn President Trump's ban on their reporting
from the White House.
They say it is a blatant violation of the First Amendment.
They and other media organizations, including NPR and Fox News, are refusing to take audio,
video, or photos from White House events until further notice.
Trump airs David Falkenflick says the Justice Department complained about news coverage
the Trump administration found unflattering and did not like.
The Justice Department referred to White House memos on this saying that they were upset
over coverage of the White House ballroom construction.
They were upset about the reports of depletion of ammunition during the war against Iran.
They were upset, for example, about coverage of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas
saying that it was unpopular and hadn't gone well, they said these things jeopardized national
security and spread falsehoods.
NPR's David Falkenflick reporting.
Voters are less confident that the U.S. Postal Service will deliver mail-in ballots on time
this year than they were in 2024.
That's according to the latest NPR/PBS/Marist poll.
NPR's Hansi Lo Wang reports.
Compared to two years ago, the share of registered voters who say they are confident or very confident
that the U.S. Postal Service will deliver mail-in ballots and other election mail-on
time has dropped 13 percentage points.
It's now down to 58 percent of voters.
That's going to an NPR/PBS/Marist poll conducted this month just as the Supreme Court blocked
the Trump administration from using USPS to restrict mail-in voting for the midterm election.
We should note USPS is a financial support of NPR.
The Postal Service is now expected to keep delivering election mail as originally planned.
In a statement, USPS says misinformation may have had an impact on public sentiment and
that it has delivered more than 200 million pieces of election mail this year with an
on-time score of close to 98 percent.
Hansi Lo Wang, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR.
The U.S. Supreme Court will, for the third time, take up a congressional redistricting
map in Missouri.
Lower court judges have approved a new map that favors Republican candidates, but the
high court has refused to agree and has deferred to the Missouri State Supreme Court.
The Missouri State Supreme Court has blocked the redistricting map from being used in this
year's midterm elections.
The Supreme Court has denied a request to intervene in a multi-state custody battle
over a newborn with a heart defect.
From member station KERA, Tollewana Osabamowo reports, the court rejected a surrogate mother's
appeal to keep the newborn.
Surrogate McKenna West left Alaska for Texas in July to give birth to a California couple's
genetic child.
The couple had asked West to get an abortion months earlier after doctors detected a severe
fetal heart abnormality.
West argues she's the child's mother under Texas law.
Earlier this month, a Dallas judge upheld a California court's order establishing the
couple as the child's parents.
West unsuccessfully asked Justice Elena Kagan, who handles appeals from California, to overturn
the order.
Last week, the Texas Supreme Court cleared the way for the newborn's genetic parents
to take him back to California for medical care.
For NPR News, I'm Tollewana Osabamowo in Dallas.
The U.S. military says an F-16 fighter jet crashed yesterday in Germany.
The pilot sustained injuries after ejecting from the aircraft.
Officials at the U.S. Air Base in western Germany say the cause of the jet crash is being investigated.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News.
Want to hear this podcast without sponsor breaks? Amazon Prime members can listen to
NPR News now, sponsor free through Amazon Music.
Or you can also support NPR's vital journalism and get NPR+ at plus dot NPR dot org.
That's plus dot NPR dot org.

topics.text: China's leader Xi Jinping will meet President Trump tomorrow in Washington
Federal judge holds hearing on media organizations' lawsuit against Trump's White House reporting ban
Voters less confident U.S. Postal Service will deliver mail-in ballots on time this year
U.S. Supreme Court will take up congressional redistricting map in Missouri for third time
Supreme Court denies surrogate mother's appeal in multi-state custody battle over newborn with heart defect
U.S. military F-16 fighter jet crashed in Germany, pilot injured after ejecting
